RagShortTexts: Yuri II was defeated and killed on the Sit in 1238 during the Mongol invasion.
Princely forces and threatened towns were separated, delaying news and assistance.

Variants.Content: In 1238 Mongol forces defeated the troops gathered with Yuri II near the Sit, killing the prince. Vladimir and other towns suffered in the same invasion. People awaiting relief inside a town and men campaigning outside it faced different dangers. Some waited without news; others found a following that had lost its lord. Dynastic households arranged succession and defence while ordinary families searched for missing people and a place to remain.

Yuri’s death required new recognition of lands and followers. A lord assessing relief asks whether a messenger actually saw the other force and whether provisions remain at the meeting place. Kinship alone cannot answer either question.

Soldiers associate the Sit with encountering an enemy before assembly is complete. Keeping contact, scouting and agreeing where scattered men should meet are practical tasks; a survivor need not know why every other contingent was absent.

Families may receive news of a fallen town and a defeated army without learning where relatives are. Shelter and food for displaced people, seed reserves and neighbourly help make another season possible.
